steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper giving a comprehensive empirical (mainly extrinsic) evaluation of existing word embedding approaches. Explain why word embeddings matter, intrinsic vs. extrinsic evaluation and the gaps in previous comparisons, what a good word representation should handle, what we study, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Word embeddings: importance and ways to build them; intrinsic vs. extrinsic evaluators
2. Semantic vs. syntactic relatedness
3. Limits of intrinsic evaluation; value of extrinsic evaluation
4. Gaps in previous comparative studies
5. What a good word representation should handle
6. What this paper does and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Word embeddings
- dense real-valued word vectors essential to NLP: question answering, semantic role labeling, textual entailment, machine translation
- encode semantic + syntactic characteristics -> input features for sentiment analysis, rumor detection, fake news detection
- lots of research on getting them from unlabeled text: statistical models, neural network language models, log-bilinear models, context-based neural models
- which approach for a specific scenario? unanswered
- compare with intrinsic or extrinsic evaluators; intrinsic = semantic/syntactic relationships directly; extrinsic = downstream tasks with embeddings as input features

2. Relatedness
- semantically related: closer meaning, should lie closer in embedding space; bicycle, cycle, bike
- syntactically related: bound by syntax of a language like English; brief / briefly (adverb of adjective); big / bigger (comparative)

3. Intrinsic vs. extrinsic
- most studies intrinsic; shows similarities but not when one model is superior/inferior
- intrinsic needs extra resources: pre-defined queries for subjective tests; word couplets (adjectives + comparatives, countries + capitals) = query inventories
- extrinsic: may be computationally expensive and time taking, but more insight into quality
- compare on real-world use cases
- small factors (window size, data pre-processing, skewness of dataset, embedding dimension) can affect downstream results (e.g. classification)

4. Gaps
- relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic investigated but not comprehensive
- not all models evaluated: mostly LSA, word2vec, GloVe
- no extensive extrinsic evaluation of all state-of-the-art models (GloVe, Word2vec, ELMo, BERT, fasttext)

5. Good word representation
- most frequent words (the, and) shouldn't affect vector quality
- rare words should get quality representations
- multiple embeddings for multiple word senses
- features should work in different scenarios, e.g. sentiment analysis with balanced and unbalanced data

6. This paper
- pre-trained vectors from dominant algorithms, different classification scenarios
- train embeddings from scratch -> effect of pre-training per algorithm
- model parameters: window size, embedding dimensions
- external parameters: formality of pre-training corpora, amount of text, pre-processing
- organization: Sec 2 existing models (traditional + neural); Sec 3 properties and comparison; Sec 4 results, pre-trained and trained; Sec 5 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dense real-valued word vector representations have been essential for NLP tasks like question answering, semantic role labeling, textual entailment and machine translation. These word representations are also called word embeddings, and they encode semantic and syntactic characteristics of the words, so they can be used as input features for downstream tasks like sentiment analysis, rumor detection, and fake news detection. Since the early days of natural language understanding, a huge amount of research has gone into getting these word representations from a corpus of unlabeled text. Researchers have used statistical models, neural network language models, log-bilinear models, and context-based neural models, among others, to build these word representations. But the question of which approach to use in a specific scenario is still unanswered. To compare word embedding methods, we can use intrinsic or extrinsic evaluators. Intrinsic evaluators measure the quality of word embeddings directly by using the semantic and syntactic relationships among them, and extrinsic evaluators measure the quality of the embeddings on downstream tasks where they are used as input features.

Words that are closer in meaning to each other are called semantically related terms, and their embeddings should lie closer together in the embedding space. For example, bicycle, cycle, and bike are similar words and are semantically related to each other. Syntactically related words are words that are bound by the syntax of a natural language like English. For example, brief and briefly are syntactically related, since briefly is the adverb for the adjective brief. Big and bigger are also syntactically related, because bigger is the comparative form of big.

Most studies look at word embedding models in terms of their intrinsic characteristics. Intrinsic evaluation of these models tells us about the semantic and syntactic similarities among the words, but it does not explicitly show the scenarios where one model is better or worse than the others. Also, intrinsic evaluators need additional resources in the form of pre-defined queries for subjective tests. These queries can be word couplets, like adjectives and their comparative forms, or countries and their capitals, and they are also called query inventories.

Extrinsic evaluation of these methods, on the other hand, may be computationally expensive and take a lot of time, but it gives much more insight into the quality of the word representations that the methods extract. To evaluate the real quality of these methods, we should compare them on their real-world use cases. Small factors like the window size, data pre-processing, skewness of the dataset, and the dimension of the word embeddings can sometimes have an impact on the result of downstream tasks (e.g., classification).

- relationship intrinsic/extrinsic studied but not comprehensively
- comparisons don't cover all models: mostly LSA, word2vec, GloVe
- no extensive extrinsic evaluation with all state-of-the-art models (GloVe, Word2vec, ELMo, BERT, fasttext)
- good representation: frequent words (the, and) shouldn't affect quality; rare words get quality vectors; multiple embeddings for multiple senses
- features should work in different scenarios, e.g. sentiment analysis with balanced and unbalanced data
- this paper: pre-trained vectors on classification scenarios; train from scratch for effect of pre-training; window size and embedding dimensions; external parameters (formality of corpora, amount of text, pre-processing)
- organization: Sec 2 existing models; Sec 3 properties + comparison; Sec 4 results (pre-trained and trained); Sec 5 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Dense real-valued word vector representations have been essential for NLP tasks like question answering, semantic role labeling, textual entailment and machine translation. These word representations are also called word embeddings, and they encode semantic and syntactic characteristics of the words, so they can be used as input features for downstream tasks like sentiment analysis, rumor detection, and fake news detection. Since the early days of natural language understanding, a huge amount of research has gone into getting these word representations from a corpus of unlabeled text. Researchers have used statistical models, neural network language models, log-bilinear models, and context-based neural models, among others, to build these word representations. But the question of which approach to use in a specific scenario is still unanswered. To compare word embedding methods, we can use intrinsic or extrinsic evaluators. Intrinsic evaluators measure the quality of word embeddings directly by using the semantic and syntactic relationships among them, and extrinsic evaluators measure the quality of the embeddings on downstream tasks where they are used as input features.

Words that are closer in meaning to each other are called semantically related terms, and their embeddings should lie closer together in the embedding space. For example, bicycle, cycle, and bike are similar words and are semantically related to each other. Syntactically related words are words that are bound by the syntax of a natural language like English. For example, brief and briefly are syntactically related, since briefly is the adverb for the adjective brief. Big and bigger are also syntactically related, because bigger is the comparative form of big.

Most studies look at word embedding models in terms of their intrinsic characteristics. Intrinsic evaluation of these models tells us about the semantic and syntactic similarities among the words, but it does not explicitly show the scenarios where one model is better or worse than the others. Also, intrinsic evaluators need additional resources in the form of pre-defined queries for subjective tests. These queries can be word couplets, like adjectives and their comparative forms, or countries and their capitals, and they are also called query inventories.

Extrinsic evaluation of these methods, on the other hand, may be computationally expensive and take a lot of time, but it gives much more insight into the quality of the word representations that the methods extract. To evaluate the real quality of these methods, we should compare them on their real-world use cases. Small factors like the window size, data pre-processing, skewness of the dataset, and the dimension of the word embeddings can sometimes have an impact on the result of downstream tasks (e.g., classification).

Researchers have investigated the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic evaluators, but these investigations have not been comprehensive. Also, these comparative studies have not evaluated all the existing models, since most studies only looked at LSA, word2vec, and GloVe. And as far as we know, there has been no extensive extrinsic evaluation that includes all the state-of-the-art models (GloVe, Word2vec, ELMo, BERT and fasttext).

A good word representation method should take care of some essential points.

- The most frequent words like the or and should not affect the quality of the word vectors.

- Rare words should also get quality word representations.

- Multiple word embeddings for multiple word senses.

Apart from these qualities, which are intrinsic to the word embeddings, the features that these models extract should work well in different scenarios; for example, for sentiment analysis the features should work fine with both balanced and unbalanced data. In this paper we use pre-trained vectors, trained with the dominant word representation algorithms, for different scenarios of classification tasks. We also train word embeddings with these algorithms from scratch, to measure the effect of pre-training for each algorithm in various tasks. We also study how the model parameters (window size and embedding dimensions) affect the output of the downstream tasks. We also study the effect of external parameters on the output of these models. The external parameters are how formal the corpora used for pre-training are, how much text is in the pre-training corpus, and pre-processing. The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 introduces the existing word representation models, both traditional and neural. In section 3 we present the properties of word embedding models and compare the existing models by these properties. Section 4 reports the results. We did exhaustive comparisons on both pre-trained and trained word embeddings. Finally, section 5 concludes our findings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Dense real-valued word vector representations have been essential to NLP tasks, such as question answering [1,2], semantic role labeling [3,4,5], textual entailment [6] and machine translation [7]. These word representations, also called word embeddings, encode semantic and syntactic characteristics of the words, so they can act as input features to downstream tasks like sentiment analysis [8,9], rumor detection [10], and fake news detection [11]. Since the early days of natural language understanding, an exhaustive amount of research has been put into obtaining these word representations from a corpus of unlabeled text. Researchers have used statistical models [12,13], neural network language models [14], log-bilinear models [15], and context-based neural models [16,17], among others, to construct these word representations. Nevertheless, the question of which approach to use in a specific scenario remains unanswered. To compare word embedding methods, we can use intrinsic or extrinsic evaluators [18]. Intrinsic evaluators measure the quality of word embeddings directly using the semantic and syntactic relationships among them [19], while extrinsic evaluators measure their quality on downstream tasks that use them as input features.

Words with closer meaning to each other are called semantically related terms, and the embeddings produced for such words should lie closer in the embedding space. For example, words like bicycle, cycle, and bike are similar and semantically related to each other. Syntactically related words are words bound by the syntax of a natural language such as English. For example, brief and briefly are syntactically related, where briefly is the adverb for the adjective brief. Likewise, big and bigger are syntactically related, where the latter is the comparative form of the former.

Most studies investigate word embedding models with respect to their intrinsic characteristics. Although intrinsic evaluation sheds light on the semantic and syntactic similarities among words, it does not explicitly depict scenarios where one model is superior or inferior to others. Moreover, intrinsic evaluators require additional resources in the form of pre-defined queries for subjective tests [20]. These queries can be word couplets, such as adjectives and their comparative forms, or countries and their capitals, and are also called query inventories [21].

Extrinsic evaluation, on the other hand, may be computationally expensive and time-consuming, but it provides much more insight into the quality of the word representations these methods extract. To evaluate the actual quality of these methods, we should compare them with regard to their real-world use cases. Small factors like the window size, data pre-processing, skewness of the dataset, and dimension of the word embeddings sometimes have an impact on the result of downstream tasks (e.g., classification) [22].

Researchers have investigated the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic evaluators, but not comprehensively [23]. Besides, these comparative studies have not evaluated all the existing models, as most studies focused only on LSA, word2vec, and GloVe [24,25,26]. Furthermore, to our knowledge, there has been no extensive extrinsic evaluation that involves all the state-of-the-art models (GloVe, Word2vec, ELMo, BERT and fasttext).

An excellent word representation method should take care of some essential points.

- The most frequent words such as the or and should not affect the quality of the word vectors.

- Rare words should have quality word representations.

- Multiple word embeddings for multiple word senses.

Apart from the above qualities, intrinsic to the word embeddings, the features extracted by these models should work well in different scenarios; for example, in sentiment analysis the features should work with both balanced and unbalanced data. In this paper, we use pre-trained vectors, trained using the dominant word representation algorithms, for different scenarios of classification tasks. We also train word embeddings with these algorithms from scratch to measure the effect of pre-training for each algorithm in various tasks. In addition, we study the impact of model parameters (window size and embedding dimensions) on the output of the downstream tasks, as well as the effect of external parameters: the degree of formality of the corpora used for pre-training, the amount of text in the pre-training corpus, and pre-processing. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces existing word representation models, including traditional and neural models. Section 3 presents the properties of word embedding models and compares the existing models according to these properties. Section 4 reports the results of our exhaustive comparisons on both pre-trained and trained word embeddings. Finally, section 5 concludes our findings.
